**Visual Analysis:**

- **Affected plant part:** Wheat heads/spikes
- **Key features:**
  - Multiple wheat heads show dark brown-to-black masses entirely replacing the normal grain/spikelet tissue
  - The rachis (central axis) remains visible but all grain tissue is replaced by dark, dusty spore masses
  - The dark material appears partially dispersed, consistent with teliospore release
  - Leaves and stems appear largely healthy/green
  - Several adjacent heads show the same pattern — systemic infection visible across multiple spikes

**Reasoning through classes:**

- **Loose Smut** (*Ustilago tritici*): Classic presentation — the fungus infects the ovary during flowering, and at heading the entire grain is replaced by olive-black spore masses covered by a fragile membrane that ruptures early, releasing dusty spores and leaving a bare rachis. This matches perfectly.
- **Dwarf Bunt**: Individual grain bunt balls, not total spike replacement
- **Head Scab**: Bleached/pink spikelets, not dark powdery masses
- **Stem Rust / Stripe Rust**: Pustules on leaves/stems, not head replacement
- **Wheat Streak Mosaic Virus**: Mosaic/yellowing patterns on leaves

The complete replacement of grain tissue with dispersing dark spore masses on the heads, with intact rachis remaining, is the hallmark of **Loose Smut**.

This is the classic presentation of Loose Smut (Ustilago tritici), where the entire head is converted to teliospores that disperse at heading time. Leaves and stems appear healthy, ruling out foliar diseases. The pattern is inconsistent with Head Scab (which shows bleached spikelets), Dwarf Bunt (individual bunt balls), or rust diseases (pustules on leaves/stems)."}
